title: Not Knowing What to Pray For
english: …our weaknesses, and so on (Romans 8:26). “But the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). It is our own spirit, plainly, that intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words; for at times we groan when we are eager to make our supplications to God. So this too we learn in the Holy Spirit, for the Spirit is wise, just as the Son is.

But since he says, “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26), let us look into this. And yet we have already been taught by Christ how we ought to pray, for he says plainly, “Pray, then, like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as in heaven” (Matthew 6:9–10), and all that follows. Since, then, we know the fitting way to make our supplications, tell me, what would be the sense of the apostle’s words? Or at what would the words spoken through Paul’s voice be aimed?

We say, then, that we do pray, seeking to ask for good things, and before all else for what serves the glory of God, and for the things by which we may live rightly and achieve a life that is truly approved. But “having the firstfruits of the Spirit, we ourselves also groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of the body” (Romans 8:23); and it is in this respect, at least, that “we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26). For if “no eye has seen and no ear has heard, nor has it entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9), what shall we ask for when we draw near? Or how could we know what we have not seen, or rather, things that lie beyond the mind and are not known to human hearts? What the redemption of the body will be, or what its refashioning is, and how it is re-formed into incorruption and glory, only he who is the craftsman of these things would know.

The Savior’s disciple, too, said somewhere to some who did not know how to pray as they ought, “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your pleasures” (James 4:3). It would therefore be quite fitting, and with good reason, for those in such a state to say, “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26). So with groanings too deep for words we ask in the spirit for things that we believe will come to be, though we are wholly ignorant of the manner in which they will come.

“We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to purpose” (Romans 8:28). All things do work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to purpose. But according to whose purpose? And what is meant by “according to purpose”? “According to purpose” would mean “according to will.” Then according to whose will have those under discussion been called: that of the one who called them, or also that of those who were called? Now every longing that carries us toward righteousness would come to us from God the Father; for Christ said somewhere (John 6:44), “No one can come to…

The row opens mid-lemma: ταῖς ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν κ.τ.λ. completes Ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα συναντιλαμβάνεται at the end of u07-open, so the English opens with an ellipsis; κ.τ.λ. rendered “and so on”. It ends mid-quotation (John 6:44), completed at the start of u07-rem-mid; the closing ellipsis marks the break. Nothing supplied.

Spirit in the Romans 8:26 lemma is capitalised as Scripture and to match the end of u07-open. Cyril then glosses it as τὸ ἡμῶν δηλονότι πνεῦμα, “our own spirit, plainly”, and says this too is learned “in the Holy Spirit”; ἐν πνεύματι in “we ask in the spirit” is left lowercase because it follows that gloss of the human spirit.
σοφὸν γάρ ἐστι καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Υἱός: the neuter σοφόν agrees with Πνεῦμα; rendered “the Spirit is wise, just as the Son is”.
τὴν εὐδόκιμον ἀληθῶς κατορθῶσαι ζωήν: εὐδόκιμος means well-approved; rendered “a life that is truly approved”; Cyril does not name who approves, so “to God” is not added.
ἀναστοιχειοῦται: literally “is re-elemented”; rendered “is re-formed”. Its subject is the body from the previous clause, given as “it”.
κατὰ πρόθεσιν is kept as “according to purpose” without “his”, because Cyril goes on to ask whose purpose is meant (the caller's or the called's).

title: Foreknowledge Wrongs No One
english: …me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Yet in this matter one would not miss what is fitting if one said that some have been called according to purpose, both the purpose of the one who called them and their own. “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed,” and so on (Romans 8:29). Many, he says, are called according to purpose, but not all are chosen (Matthew 22:14); only those have been honored who were also foreknown as those who would be conformed to the image of his Son.

What the image of his Son should be understood to be, the blessed Paul himself will make clear again, saying, “For just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Corinthians 15:49). For those who have paid no heed to fleshly desires are the ones who have imitated the image of Christ, that is, the way of life and conduct that is in holiness. For just as we say that the image of the man of dust, that is, of Adam, is the life lived in disobedience and sins, so too the image of the heavenly one, that is, of Christ, is holiness, justification and obedience. All, then, who were foreknown as those who would, in their own times, be conformed to the life of Christ and be its imitators, so far as human nature allows, these have also been called. “And those whom he predestined he also called; and those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30).

It is not at all unlikely that some, carried away by ignorance, should make this matter a ready pretext for unbelief and say, “If those whom he foreknew according to purpose and predestined are the ones who have been called, it has nothing to do with us who have not yet believed; for we have not been called, nor have we been predestined.” To them we will say that the one who gave the wedding feast for his son sent his servants to gather those who had been called, but they would not come (Matthew 22:2–3). After them, those who were called according to their own purpose came in, and so the wedding hall was filled with guests (Matthew 22:10). So nothing is seen standing in the way of those who are willing to come. Foreknowledge does no wrong to anyone at all, nor does it give anyone an advantage. Otherwise, let them teach us whether those who in their disobedience outraged the God who called them were not foreknown as well. More than that, some were called and rushed into the wedding, yet they did not become chosen, nor were they justified or glorified. For what reason? Because they were not wearing a garment fit for the wedding (Matthew 22:11–12).

Besides, we shall find our Lord Jesus Christ himself saying openly, “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). See, he was already calling all people to himself, and no one would be without a share in the grace of being called; for in saying “all” he sends no one away at all. “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:31–32). For those who have chosen to do good, all things work together, since God shields them. For he who did not spare the one who is his Son by nature, so that he might save those in danger and…

The row opens mid-quotation (με, ἐὰν μὴ ὁ Πατὴρ ... completes John 6:44 from u07-rem-early) and ends mid-sentence at ἵνα σώσῃ κινδυνεύοντας, καί; ἀπαλλάξῃ κινδύνων and the main clause follow in u07-rem-close. Ellipses mark both joins; nothing supplied.
τήν τε τοῦ κεκληκότος καὶ τὴν ἑαυτῶν: the feminine article picks up πρόθεσιν; rendered “both the purpose of the one who called them and their own”.
φησίν in “Many, he says, are called”: Cyril reports Paul's sense in words drawn from Matthew 22:14, not a quotation of Romans.
προορίζω rendered “predestine” throughout, the usual English for Romans 8:29–30.
τοὺς κεκλημένους in the parable rendered “those who had been called” (not “invited”) to keep Cyril's play on κλητοί / κέκληνται.
ἀδικεῖ δὲ οὐδένα τὸ σύμπαν ἡ πρόγνωσις, οὔτε μὴν ὀνίνησί τινας: foreknowledge neither harms nor helps; ὀνίνησι rendered “give anyone an advantage”, keeping the negation exact.
ἐπεὶ διδασκόντων: ἐπεί with a third-person imperative, “otherwise, let them teach us”; Cyril's point is that the disobedient were also foreknown, so foreknowledge did not cause their refusal.
τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ... Υἱοῦ: “the one who is his Son by nature”, keeping Cyril's term against adoptive sonship.
PG column numbers 221 and 222 and the page number 20 are dropped; the split word τού τους is read as τούτους.

title: Paul’s Grief for Israel
english: …set them free from dangers, how will he not also, with him, give us all things (Romans 8:32)? “Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen? It is God who justifies; who is the one who condemns?” (Romans 8:33–34). Perhaps Paul, with a wise purpose, does not let the minds of the called fall into helplessness, but teaches that they will be set free from their former sins and will be justified, as God grants it. For although every sin involves a transgression of the divine law and condemns the careless, yet if the Lord of the law himself forgives, who is the one who condemns the sinner?

“I am speaking the truth in Christ, I am not lying; my conscience bears witness with me” (Romans 9:1). In the beginning God made Israel his chosen one and even called him firstborn (Exodus 4:22). But they became boastful and insolent, and, what goes beyond even this, slayers of the Lord. That is why they have perished; for they have been sent away and cast out, and, having slipped wholly from their closeness to God, they have been placed behind the nations; and they have shown themselves strangers to the hope of the fathers.

Now the blessed Paul had been appointed a minister of the divine gospel and was proclaiming Jesus to the nations. Again and again he said that those of Israel’s blood had fallen away, and he insisted that those who were once in darkness and served demons had become called according to the purpose and foreknowledge of God. So that none of the less instructed might think he was all but leaping on his own kin as they lay fallen, and smiling over their fall, he makes a necessary defense and says, “I am speaking the truth in Christ, I am not lying,” and what follows (Romans 9:1).

Over those who have gone so far in perversity as to slip from their love for God, and then to suffer harsh penalties for it, one might well grieve; and to shed a tear for them out of fellow feeling would not be beyond reason; or rather, it is the fullness of love. But to wish even to be accursed from Christ on their behalf (Romans 9:3) goes beyond the measures of love. For no one, if he is in his right mind, would choose to offend God for the sake of the salvation of others, counting his own life as nothing while choosing that others should have it.

What, then, does he mean in putting forward his own salvation as the price of the salvation of the Jews? The statement is a hyperbole, and it gives proof of the most perfect love. “For I could wish,” he says, “that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers” (Romans 9:3). It is as if he were saying, “If Israel were saved by my offending Christ, I myself would have chosen it.” He who said to those justified in faith, “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2); he who proclaims to all, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?” (Romans 8:35): to undergo so dreadful an evil, and one on behalf of…

The row opens mid-sentence: ἀπαλλάξῃ κινδύνων completes ἵνα σώσῃ κινδυνεύοντας, καί from u07-rem-mid, so the English opens with an ellipsis. It ends mid-sentence at καὶ εἷς ὑπέρ; the phrase continues in u08-open (πάντων χωρῆσαι πρὸς ὄλεθρον). The long sentence has no finite main verb in the source; the closing infinitives are kept as they stand and nothing is supplied.
οἰκονομικῶς: “with a wise purpose” (with pastoral design, by way of the economy); Θεοῦ κατανεύοντος: “as God grants it”.
ὁ τοῦ νόμου Κύριος: God as Lord of the law; capitalised.
κυριοκτόνοι: Cyril's own polemical term, “slayers of the Lord”, translated as it stands, not softened or sharpened.

λειτουργὸς τῶν θείων εὐαγγελίων: the plural εὐαγγέλια rendered “the divine gospel” (the message, not the four books); possible echo of Romans 15:16 (λειτουργὸν Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ εἰς τὰ ἔθνη), not cited inline because the wording differs.
τοὺς ἐν σκότῳ ποτέ: possible echo of Ephesians 5:8 (ἦτε γάρ ποτε σκότος); not cited inline because the wording differs.
μᾶλλον δὲ τῆς ἀγάπης τὴν πλήρωσιν ἔχει: “or rather, it is the fullness of love”; not cited as Romans 13:10, whose wording (πλήρωμα νόμου ἡ ἀγάπη) and sense differ.
ἑτέροις γεμὴν τὸ χρῆμα ἐνεῖναι ἑλεῖν: τὸ χρῆμα (“the thing”) refers back to τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ζωήν; rendered “while choosing that others should have it”.
τὴν ἑαυτοῦ (sc. σωτηρίαν) as ἀντάλλαγμα: “his own salvation as the price of the salvation of the Jews”.
ηὐχόμην rendered “I could wish”, the usual English for the imperfect in Romans 9:3.
